about: Curated Game Updates and Historical Events for Story Mode (GLOSSARY: Game Update, Historical Event, Main Circuit). DRAFT for review. Facts are restated in our own words; 'source' names the archived Liquipedia page (CC-BY-SA 3.0) the fact comes from, a Wikipedia article (also CC-BY-SA), or the tournament map pools in the archive. 'precision' says how exact the date is (day, month, year); 'window' brackets a change we only know happened between two dated events. Bans and deaths are not listed here: events.py generates them from the banned-player lists and player pages (only the headline cases appear below). Map pools only list the maps that exist in the game (map pools option B): Dust, Inferno, Mirage, Nuke, Overpass, Ancient, Train, Anubis, Cache.

effects_vocabulary.version: the Main Circuit moves to this game version
effects_vocabulary.form_shock: every player's form is briefly disrupted (0..1)
effects_vocabulary.weights: multiplies how much an attribute counts in match strength (1.0 = unchanged), until a later update changes it
effects_vocabulary.map_pool: add / remove / set the competitive map pool
effects_vocabulary.map_rework: these maps changed: every team's familiarity with them drops
effects_vocabulary.prize_scale: multiplies prize money and sponsor income (with 'until' when it is temporary)
effects_vocabulary.comeback: multiplies the chance of winning rounds while behind
effects_vocabulary.youth_talent: multiplies how many new talents appear
effects_vocabulary.talent_drain: share of players leaving the Main Circuit (for another game or league)
effects_vocabulary.unpaid_prizes: this organizer stops paying prize money
effects_vocabulary.organizer_closed: this organizer's events leave the calendar
effects_vocabulary.major_teams: number of teams at a Major
effects_vocabulary.invites: how big events invite teams: strength (Strength Ranking), minors, rmr, vrs

entries.title: Counter-Strike 1.0 leaves beta
entries.detail: The retail release ends a year of public betas. Competitive play had already begun on the betas.

entries.title: Lag compensation netcode
entries.detail: Valve's new netcode makes high-ping play far more even, so online results start to reflect real skill.

entries.title: The Major era begins (CPL Winter 2001)
entries.detail: Until 2012 the biggest events, the 'majors', are CPL Winter/Summer, ESWC, WCG and later the IEM World Championship. They are not Valve-funded.

entries.title: DreamHack becomes twice a year
entries.detail: DreamHack Summer (June) joins DreamHack Winter (late November), and both become fixtures of the calendar.

entries.title: Counter-Strike 1.6 beta on Steam
entries.detail: 1.6 adds the FAMAS, Galil and tactical shield, plus a new Inferno.

entries.title: First Electronic Sports World Cup
entries.detail: ESWC joins CPL and WCG as a major.

entries.title: Steam launches: 1.6 becomes the standard
entries.detail: The final 1.6 ships with the Steam client after a beta that ended on September 9. Updates now arrive automatically, and the scene settles on 1.6.

entries.title: Counter-Strike: Source beta
entries.detail: A parallel Source scene forms. The Main Circuit stays on 1.6, but some players leave for Source.

entries.title: CPL World Tour: the first $1,000,000 circuit
entries.detail: A season-long tour with a million dollars in prizes. Pro CS becomes worth more money for one year.

entries.title: Intel leaves the CPL; WSVG and IEM are born
entries.detail: Intel funds the new World Series of Video Games and turns ESL's European league into the Intel Extreme Masters. KODE5 and the Championship Gaming Invitational also start this year.
entries.source: WSVG; Intel Extreme Masters; KODE5; Championship Gaming Series

entries.title: Championship Gaming Series draft
entries.detail: DirecTV's franchise league drafts players onto city teams with salaries. Some players leave their clans for the CGS.

entries.title: KODE5 stops paying prizes
entries.detail: From 2008 on, KODE5 winners are not paid. By 2012 the debt to teams passes $100,000.

entries.title: CPL shuts down its events
entries.detail: The CPL ceases operations, citing a crowded field of leagues; it is sold to an Abu Dhabi group in August.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Cyberathlete Professional League; CPL (sale on 2008-08-25)

entries.title: Global financial crisis
entries.detail: The recession hits esports sponsors; leagues fold and prize pools shrink until 2010.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Championship Gaming Series (the recession is cited in its shutdown)
entries.status: confirmed (context); the size of the effect is our estimate

entries.title: Championship Gaming Series folds
entries.detail: DirecTV's league announces its shutdown in the recession; its players are free agents again.

entries.title: ESWC changes hands; no ESWC in 2009
entries.detail: Games-Solution buys the brand and the 2009 edition is not held. ESWC returns in 2010.
entries.source: Electronic Sports World Cup; Counter-Strike Majors

entries.title: Natus Vincere founded
entries.detail: The Ukrainian organization that dominates 2010 is formed.

entries.title: World e-Sports Masters drops Counter-Strike
entries.detail: 2010 is the last WEM with CS.

entries.title: ESL prize payment controversy
entries.detail: ESL comes under scrutiny for paying prizes late.

entries.title: Last 1.6 major (IEM Season VI)
entries.detail: 1.6 is winding down; most organizers drop it within the year.

entries.title: Counter-Strike: Global Offensive released
entries.detail: The Main Circuit moves to CS:GO over the next months. Movement, spray patterns and economy all change, so expect upsets while teams adapt.
entries.source: Counter-Strike: Global Offensive; pool from DreamHack Winter 2013

entries.title: DreamHack, MLG and ESL partner
entries.detail: The three organizers coordinate their circuits in Europe and North America.

entries.title: ESL Major Series for CS:GO
entries.detail: ESL's first premier CS:GO competition, with finals in Cologne.

entries.title: Arms Deal update: weapon skins
entries.detail: Skins bring money into the game; sponsorship in CS:GO starts to grow.

entries.title: First Valve Major: DreamHack Winter 2013 ($250,000)
entries.detail: Valve-funded Majors become the top of the calendar; 16 teams, GSL groups.

entries.title: Overpass (and Cobblestone) added to the game
entries.detail: Not yet in the competitive pool.

entries.title: Mirage, Inferno and Dust II reworked
Overpass and Cache join the pool; Train leaves
entries.detail: Cobblestone also joins, but it is not in the game. The Cologne 2014 pool: Dust II, Inferno, Mirage, Nuke, Overpass, Cache, Cobblestone.
entries.source: Overpass; tournament map pools (DreamHack Summer 2014, ESL One Cologne 2014)
entries.status: confirmed (Overpass on July 1; DreamHack Summer 2014 still used the old pool)

entries.title: Tec-9 accuracy buff
entries.detail: Better accuracy and less recoil make T-side pistol buys stronger.

entries.title: VAC ban wave hits pro players
entries.detail: Several professional players are banned for cheating (generated ban events).

entries.title: iBUYPOWER match-fixing bans
entries.detail: Valve bans the players involved in the 2014 match-fixing case from its events.

entries.title: Train returns; Nuke leaves
entries.source: tournament map pools (ESL Pro League Season 1, 99Damage Arena 5, DreamHack Tours 2015)

entries.title: ESL ESEA Pro League announced ($1,000,000)
entries.detail: A season-based league for Europe and North America with a million dollars in prizes over two seasons.

entries.title: Modern Times Group buys ESL
entries.detail: Big media money enters CS:GO; prize pools grow.

entries.title: Animation and hitbox overhaul; M4A1-S changed
entries.detail: New player animations and hitboxes change how fights feel.

entries.title: Valve introduces Minor Championships
entries.detail: Regional Minors become the qualifying route to the Majors.

entries.title: Operation Wildfire: the new Nuke
entries.detail: Nuke is rebuilt from scratch; teams must relearn it.

entries.title: Major prize pool rises to $1,000,000 (MLG Columbus)
Nuke returns; Inferno leaves for rework
entries.source: tournament map pools (DreamHack Austin 2016, DreamHack Tours 2016, ELEAGUE Season 1)

entries.title: ELEAGUE starts on TBS
entries.detail: CS:GO on US cable television.

entries.title: Inferno overhaul
entries.detail: New look and layout changes, including the reopened T-spawn exit.

entries.title: PEA dispute: players refuse to leave ESL Pro League
entries.detail: The North American team owners' association bars its players from ESL Pro League; the players push back and the PEA drops its CS:GO league.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Professional Esports Association; Open Letter to the Professional eSports Association

entries.title: Inferno returns; Dust II leaves for rework
entries.source: tournament map pools (Assembly Winter 2017, DreamHack Las Vegas 2017)

entries.title: Majors switch to a Swiss group stage
Dust II reskinned
entries.detail: Dust II's first big change in CS:GO.

entries.title: Majors grow to 24 teams (ELEAGUE Boston)
entries.detail: An offline qualifier becomes part of the Major.

entries.title: CZ75-Auto nerf; M4A1-S reserve up; MP7 cheaper
entries.detail: The CZ75 no longer one-shots a helmeted opponent.

entries.title: CS:GO goes free to play
entries.detail: The player base grows; more talent appears in the lower tiers.

entries.title: Round-loss bonus rework
entries.detail: Loss bonuses step down one level per win instead of resetting, which weakens economic snowballs. AUG and M4A1-S are also tweaked.

entries.title: Cache leaves the pool (Vertigo joins)
entries.detail: Vertigo is not in the game.

entries.title: COVID-19: LAN events move online
entries.detail: After IEM Katowice 2020 (played without a crowd) every top event is online by region until IEM Cologne 2021. The Rio Major is postponed and then cancelled in September 2020.
entries.source: IEM Katowice 2020; IEM Cologne 2021; Wikipedia: Counter-Strike Major Championships

entries.title: Flashpoint: a team-owned league
entries.detail: Teams form their own league with FACEIT, with over $2 million in prizes for 2020.

entries.title: Regional Major Rankings replace the Minors
entries.detail: During the online period, Major spots come from points earned at regional RMR events.

entries.title: ESIC opens its match-fixing investigation
entries.detail: Working with law enforcement on betting syndicates bribing lower-tier players; bans follow over the next years.

entries.title: Operation Broken Fang: Ancient released
entries.detail: Not yet in the competitive pool.

entries.title: Coach spectator bug bans
entries.detail: Coaches who abused the spectator bug are banned (generated ban events).

entries.title: First Major since 2019 (Stockholm, $2,000,000)
entries.detail: Majors return on LAN with a doubled prize pool.

entries.title: RMR becomes single events per region
entries.detail: Europe, Americas and Asia-Pacific each hold one RMR event for their Major spots.

entries.title: Anubis joins; Dust II leaves. AWP magazine cut to 5
entries.detail: The AWP magazine drops from 10 to 5 rounds and the M4A1-S loses range.

entries.title: Valve announces its Regional Standings (VRS)
entries.detail: Valve's own team ranking will seed the RMRs and Majors.

entries.title: Valve bans partner leagues from 2025
entries.detail: Tournament organizers may no longer have business ties with teams; BLAST and ESL rebuild their circuits around VRS invitations.

entries.title: Counter-Strike 2 replaces CS:GO
entries.detail: Sub-tick servers and volumetric smokes change utility play: grenades and coordination matter more. Every map is rebuilt in Source 2. Matches become MR12 (first to 13 rounds).

entries.title: Dust II returns; Overpass leaves
entries.status: confirmed (Overpass date; Dust II in the Shanghai pool)

entries.title: Train returns (CS2 version); Vertigo leaves
entries.detail: The new Train enters the competitive map groups; Majors use it from 2025. The same update adds damage prediction.

entries.title: Open circuit: VRS decides invitations
entries.detail: Announced by Valve in 2023: from 2025 no organizer may have partner teams, and only the Valve Regional Standings may be used for invitations. Events are graded Tier 1, Tier 2, Wildcard or unranked.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Counter-Strike in esports; Blast Premier; Valve Tier 1 Events

entries.title: 32-team Majors; RMRs replaced by Major Regional Qualifiers
entries.detail: Announced on January 3, 2025. The top 16 teams by the last Major and VRS are invited directly; the rest come through regional qualifiers.
entries.source: Valve Regional Standings; Regional Major Rankings

entries.title: All Major slots filled by VRS invites
entries.detail: Major Regional Qualifiers are removed; every slot comes from VRS by region.

entries.title: Overpass returns; Anubis leaves
entries.source: tournament map pools (BLAST Austin Major 2025, IEM Cologne 2025)

entries.title: Best-of-five Major grand final (StarLadder Budapest)
entries.detail: Stage 1 spots also come from VRS from this Major on.

entries.title: Anubis returns; Train leaves
entries.source: tournament map pools (StarLadder Budapest Major 2025, IEM Kraków 2026)
